fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The thread that's run through pretty much everything I've done is this question of how language connects to action, to actually doing things in the world, rather than language as a thing that just sits on a page.

Going back to my PhD days at MIT, the first work I got really excited about was getting agents to play text-based games, those old interactive fiction games where the whole world is described to you in text and you type commands back. There's no pixels, no physics engine, just words. And I found that fascinating because it forces you to confront the idea that understanding language isn't really about predicting the next token or labeling a sentence, it's about being able to use what you read to make a decision and then seeing what happens. The environment gives you feedback. That loop between reading, acting, and learning from consequences is what hooked me.

The GPT work was in some sense a detour from that, but a very productive one. We were asking a fairly simple question at the time, which was, can you learn a lot about language just from predicting text at scale and then transfer that to downstream tasks? And the answer turned out to be yes, far more than we expected. But even then, what I was most curious about was what you do with a model like that once you have it.

So these days most of my group's energy goes into what people now call language agents. Systems that take a model, give it tools, let it interact with a software environment or a web browser or a codebase, and then try to get it to accomplish real goals over many steps. Things like SWE-bench and SWE-agent came out of asking, okay, can a model actually fix a bug in a real repository, not just answer a question about code? And what I love about that space is that it's humbling. The models are impressive in isolation and then you drop them into a messy, long-horizon task and you discover all these gaps in planning, in memory, in knowing when you're wrong. Those gaps are where the interesting research is for me.

r001.rationale: The response describes his interest in language agents, real-world tasks, and research into model limitations, but does not characterize his preferred approach as closing the gap between current AI capabilities and what he envisions one or two steps ahead.

opus-5.5.text:
I think what I keep coming back to is the intersection of language and decision-making: building systems that don't just produce text but actually use language to act in the world. That thread goes all the way back to my PhD. I was working on getting agents to play text-based games, where the whole environment is described in language and you have to figure out what to do just from reading. At the time it seemed like a niche problem, but it captured something I cared about: understanding language isn't just predicting the next word. It's being able to ground it, to take actions, see the consequences, and adapt.

Then GPT came along, and the pretraining side got really exciting. Suddenly you had models with a huge amount of world knowledge and linguistic ability baked in. But I always felt that was half the story. The other half is: how do you turn that into something that can reason over multiple steps, use tools, interact with environments, recover from mistakes? So a lot of what my group has done over the last few years is on what we call language agents. That includes work on getting models to interleave reasoning and acting, getting them to explore different reasoning paths, having them reflect on their own failures, and building benchmarks like software engineering tasks or web shopping where the model has to operate in a realistic environment rather than just answer a question.

The other thing I'm drawn to, and maybe this is the professor in me, is evaluation. It's easy to build a demo that looks impressive. It's much harder to know whether a system is actually reliable when it's dealing with real users, real ambiguity, and real consequences. So I care a lot about designing environments and benchmarks that reveal where these systems break, because that's usually where the most interesting research questions are.

r001.rationale: The response describes his interest in language agents, tool use, and evaluation, but does not characterize his preferred approach as closing the gap between current AI capabilities and what he envisions one or two steps ahead.

fable-5.text:
I've always been drawn to the intersection of language and action — this idea that language isn't just something to be processed or generated in isolation, but a tool that agents can use to actually get things done in the world.

That thread goes all the way back to my PhD days. Some of my early work was on getting agents to play text-based adventure games using reinforcement learning, and later teaching machines to read instruction manuals to improve at games like Civilization. What fascinated me then, and still does now, is this question of grounding — how does language connect to perception, to decision-making, to real consequences in an environment?

So even with the GPT work, which was more about representation learning at scale, my personal motivation was always, how do we get from models that understand text to agents that can act on it? These days that's where most of my energy goes — building language agents that can navigate websites, write and debug code, use tools, and operate autonomously over long horizons. Things like benchmarks for software engineering tasks, where an agent has to actually resolve a real issue in a real codebase, not just answer a multiple-choice question.

What I love about this space is that it forces you to confront the hard problems. You can't hide behind benchmark numbers when your agent has to complete a real task — either it books the flight or it doesn't, either the code runs or it doesn't. That feedback loop between language, reasoning, and action is where I think some of the most exciting progress in AI is happening right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes moving from text understanding toward agents that act, but it does not characterize his preferred approach as closing the gap between current AI capabilities and what he envisions one or two steps ahead.

opus-5.text:
I've always been drawn to the intersection of language and decision-making. My PhD was on using text to make agents better at acting in the world — playing text games, reading manuals to learn how to play strategy games, that kind of thing. And at the time that felt like a pretty niche corner. Most of NLP was about classification, parsing, translation — tasks where you hand the model a sentence and it hands you back a label. I was more interested in language as something you *use* to get something done.

What I find exciting now is that the field has sort of caught up with that framing, but from the opposite direction. We built these enormous language models that absorbed an incredible amount of knowledge about the world, and now the open question is how you get them to actually deploy that knowledge over long horizons, in environments where they have to take actions and observe consequences and recover from mistakes. That's where a lot of my group's work has gone — things like getting a model to interleave reasoning with acting, or giving it a real codebase and a real bug report and seeing whether it can actually fix the thing.

And honestly, the part I find most interesting is the measurement problem. We're not very good at knowing what these systems can and can't do. A lot of what looks like capability is just the benchmark being easier than we thought. So I spend a surprising amount of time thinking about how to build evaluations that don't lie to us.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes interest in getting language models to use knowledge through actions and evaluating their abilities, but does not characterize this as closing the gap between current capabilities and what Narasimhan envisions one or two steps ahead.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I'm most drawn to the problem of getting language models to do things, not just say things. When we worked on the original GPT paper, the exciting question was whether pre-training on lots of text could give you a general-purpose language understanding system. That worked far better than most of us expected. But what I keep coming back to is the next step, which is turning that capability into agents that can act in an environment, whether that's a website, a codebase, or a tool with an API, and pursue goals over many steps.

That's a different kind of problem from next-token prediction. The model has to plan, notice when something went wrong, recover, and decide what information it still needs. It also has to be reliable across a long sequence of decisions, and that is where a lot of the interesting failures show up. A model can look brilliant on a single question and then fall apart on a task that takes thirty steps, because small errors compound.

So a lot of my group's work is about building benchmarks and environments that expose those failures, and then figuring out how to fix them. I find it especially satisfying because it sits between language, reasoning, and decision-making, so you can't treat it as purely an NLP problem or purely a reinforcement learning problem. You have to draw on both.

r001.rationale: The response describes moving from language models’ current text capability to the next step of agents that act in environments and pursue goals, conveying the preferred direction of closing that gap.
